qs.q: A 70-year-old man undergoes an abdominal ultrasound as part of an evaluation for lower urinary tract symptoms. Which measurement obtained during this scan is generally considered the upper limit of normal for post-void residual urine?
o: 30 mL measurement threshold
100 mL measurement threshold
10 mL measurement threshold
300 mL measurement threshold
qs.e: A normal post-void residual urine volume on abdominal ultrasound is under 30 mL. Higher volumes indicate inefficient bladder emptying secondary to outlet obstruction or detrusor failure.
qs.s: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) and Acute Urinary Retention: MCQs

qs.q: A 6-month-old infant presents with the classical triad of intussusception. An abdominal ultrasound is performed to confirm the diagnosis. Which of the following ultrasonographic findings is most characteristic on a transverse view?
o: The pseudo-kidney sign indicating mucosal oedema
A coiled spring filling defect within the caecum
The target sign or doughnut sign of concentric rings
The pseudokidney sign with absent venous flow
qs.e: The target sign or doughnut sign representing concentric rings is seen on a transverse ultrasound view of an intussusception. The pseudo-kidney sign is typically observed on longitudinal views rather than transverse views.
qs.s: Intussusception in Children: Diagnosis, Air Enema and Surgery: MCQs

qs.q: A 38-year-old man with severe sepsis and jaundice is found to have intrahepatic cholestasis without dilated ducts on his abdominal ultrasound. Which of the following best explains the absence of ductal dilatation?
o: A. Intrahepatic cholestasis lacks mechanical large duct obstruction
B. The ultrasound transducer frequency was too low to visualize ducts
C. Rapid urinary clearance prevents bilirubin accumulation in bile
D. Conjugated bilirubin bypasses the liver via portosystemic shunts
qs.e: Intrahepatic cholestasis mimics mechanical obstruction biochemically but occurs without extrahepatic or large intrahepatic duct obstruction, hence ducts remain normal on imaging. Mechanical causes like stones or pancreatic masses produce visible backpressure and duct dilatation.
qs.s: Surgical Jaundice: Obstructive Jaundice, Cholangitis and Biliary: MCQs

qs.q: A 50-year-old smoker is found to have a 3.5 cm asymptomatic solid renal mass incidentally discovered during an abdominal ultrasound for biliary colic. What is the most appropriate initial imaging step to properly characterise this lesion and assess local staging?
o: Routine core needle biopsy of the mass prior to any surgical intervention
Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis
Plain abdominal radiography with intravenous urography for visualization
Abdominal magnetic resonance imaging without intravenous contrast agents
qs.e: Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis is the main investigation to characterise an enhancing solid mass, assess its size, local extent, renal vein and IVC involvement, and check for metastasis. Routine biopsy is avoided due to seeding risk.
qs.s: Renal Masses and Renal Cell Carcinoma: MCQs

qs.q: A 45‑year‑old man with right lower quadrant pain and an Alvarado score of 5 is taken for abdominal ultrasound. Which finding would confirm acute appendicitis?
o: A non-compressible blind-ended tubular structure greater than six millimetres
Free fluid located in Morrison's pouch without any appendiceal thickening
A hyperintense cystic mass identified within the left lower iliac fossa
A fully compressible tubular structure measuring three millimetres across
qs.e: A non‑compressible blind‑ended tubular structure >6 mm is the classic ultrasound sign of acute appendicitis. A 3 mm compressible tube represents a normal appendix.
qs.s: Acute Appendicitis in Adults and Children, with the Child with Acute: MCQs

qs.q: A 48‑year‑old woman presents with right‑upper‑quadrant pain, fever, and leukocytosis. An abdominal ultrasound is ordered to evaluate for acute cholecystitis. Which sonographic finding most strongly supports the diagnosis?
o: Pericholecystic fluid collection
Gallstones larger than 1 cm
Positive sonographic Murphy's sign
Gallbladder wall thickening >3 mm
qs.e: Wall thickening >3 mm is the most specific sonographic criterion for acute cholecystitis. The other findings are supportive but not as definitive.
qs.s: Gallstones: Biliary Colic, Cholecystitis, Cholangitis and: MCQs

qs.q: A 58-year-old man undergoes an abdominal ultrasound for elevated liver enzymes, which reveals an incidental, solitary 3.5 cm gallstone. He reports no abdominal pain, fever, or gastrointestinal symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate management plan?
o: Extracorporeal shock‑wave lithotripsy (ESWL)
Oral ursodeoxycholic acid therapy
Observe with yearly ultrasound surveillance
Elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy
qs.e: Elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy is indicated for asymptomatic gallstones larger than 3 cm because of a significantly increased risk of gallbladder carcinoma. Observation with annual ultrasound imaging is incorrect because gallstones of this size carry malignant potential regardless of symptom status.
qs.s: Gallstones: Biliary Colic, Cholecystitis, Cholangitis and: MCQs

qs.q: A 64-year-old man presents to the emergency department with right upper quadrant pain, fever, and leukocytosis. He reports that his symptoms started 10 days ago. Abdominal ultrasound confirms acute calculous cholecystitis with marked local tissue edema. Which management strategy is most appropriate?
o: Percutaneous cholecystostomy drainage with discharge
Immediate laparoscopic cholecystectomy during admission
Urgent endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography
Initial conservative therapy with delayed cholecystectomy
qs.e: For acute cholecystitis presenting late (more than 7 to 10 days after symptom onset), conservative management with antibiotics followed by delayed cholecystectomy at 6 to 12 weeks is recommended because severe tissue inflammation makes early surgery technically challenging. Immediate laparoscopic cholecystectomy during the emergency admission is preferred only when patients present within the first 7 days of symptom
qs.s: Gallstones: Biliary Colic, Cholecystitis, Cholangitis and: MCQs

es.q: A 50-year-old asymptomatic patient undergoes an abdominal ultrasound for unrelated reasons, which incidentally reveals a 3 cm hyperechoic lesion in the liver. What is the most likely benign diagnosis for this lesion, and what crucial management advice would you give regarding further diagnostic proc
es.m: The most likely benign diagnosis for an incidental, hyperechoic liver lesion is a Cavernous Hemangioma (2 marks). The crucial management advice is to NOT biopsy the lesion (2 marks), due to the significant risk of hemorrhage (1 mark).

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Ultrasound is a bedside, non‑invasive tool that helps diagnose abdominal pathology, guide management, and monitor treatment in resource‑limited hospitals. It is essential for evaluating pain, jaundice, ascites, and organ size.

sections.p: Abdominal ultrasound uses high‑frequency sound waves to create real‑time images of abdominal organs. It is performed with a portable machine and a convex probe, often in the emergency or ward setting.
b: Portable machines are common; probe size 3.5–5 MHz

t.b: Normal: anechoic lumen, smooth walls; stones: echogenic foci with acoustic shadow
Homogeneous: normal; nodular: cirrhosis or focal lesions
Small: chronic disease; normal: acute process

sections.p: Ultrasound findings are staged by organ involvement and complications. For example, gallstones with cholecystitis are stage I; gangrenous cholecystitis is stage III.
In East Africa, the common causes detected by ultrasound are gallstones, hepatosplenic schistosomiasis, malaria‑related hepatomegaly, and HIV‑associated lymphadenopathy.
Patients often report right upper quadrant pain, jaundice, or abdominal distension. On exam, tenderness, Murphy’s sign, or shifting dullness may be present.
Ultrasound complements laboratory tests. When unavailable, clinical assessment and basic labs guide decisions.

t.b: Elevated ALP and GGT suggest biliary disease

sections.p: Signs of perforation, sepsis, or massive ascites require urgent surgical referral.
Treat the underlying cause: antibiotics for infection, analgesia, and surgery for obstruction or perforation. Supportive care includes fluids and monitoring.

t.b: It lacks gram‑negative coverage needed for intra‑abdominal sepsis

sections.p: Repeat ultrasound if symptoms persist. Prevention focuses on diet, vaccination, and early treatment of infections.

faq.q: When is an abdominal ultrasound indicated in a patient with jaundice?
faq.a: If jaundice is conjugated, lasts more than 14 days, or stools are pale, an ultrasound should be performed to assess biliary obstruction.

faq.q: What does a bright, well‑defined 3 cm liver lesion in a healthy woman suggest?
faq.a: It may represent a benign cyst or focal nodular hyperplasia; further imaging or biopsy may be needed.

faq.q: How do you interpret a smaller left kidney on ultrasound?
faq.a: A smaller kidney suggests chronic disease such as nephron loss; absence of cysts or masses points away from acute obstruction.

exam: A 32‑year‑old woman presents with right upper quadrant pain and a positive Murphy’s sign. What is the next best step? — Perform an abdominal ultrasound to confirm gallstones and assess for cholecystitis.
A patient with HIV has a palpable abdominal mass. Ultrasound shows a heterogeneous liver. What is the most likely diagnosis? — Hepatosplenic schistosomiasis; treat with praziquantel.

A 45‑year‑old man has fever, abdominal pain, and a tender right lower quadrant. Ultrasound is normal. What is the next step? — Repeat ultrasound or consider CT if suspicion of appendicitis remains high.
A patient with ascites has a normal ultrasound but high serum creatinine. What complication should you consider? — Renal failure due to hepatorenal syndrome.
Why is metronidazole alone avoided in intra‑abdominal infections? — It lacks coverage for gram‑negative organisms common in the gut.
A pregnant woman has right upper quadrant pain. Ultrasound shows a normal gallbladder. What is the likely cause? — Hepatitis or fatty liver; consider viral serology.
A patient with chronic abdominal pain has a small left kidney on ultrasound. What is the most probable cause? — Chronic kidney disease; manage with ACE inhibitors and monitor renal function.
What is the significance of a nodular liver surface on ultrasound? — Indicates cirrhosis; assess for portal hypertension and plan for surveillance.
